subject: Biotechnology
title: The Human Genome Project
description: Learn The Human Genome Project in one minute.

hook.text: It took 13 years and $2.7 billion to read one human genome — the largest biology project in history.

buildup.text: The Human Genome Project mapped all 3.2 billion base pairs of human DNA — letter by letter.

discovery.text: Humans have only about 20,000 genes — far fewer than expected. A rice plant has more.

twist.text: Craig Venter's private effort raced the public project — competition accelerated completion to 2003.

climax.text: Today a genome can be sequenced in hours for under $200 — a ten-million-fold cost reduction in 20 years.

punchline.text: Reading one genome took 13 years — now it takes a day.

quiz.question: How many protein-coding genes do humans have?

details.summary: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year international effort completed in 2003 that sequenced all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA. It cost approximately 3 billion dollars and provided the reference genome that underpins modern genomics and personalized medicine.
details.whyItMatters: The Human Genome Project transformed biology from studying individual genes to analyzing entire genomes. It enabled personalized medicine, accelerated drug discovery, and spawned technologies that made genomics accessible and affordable.
takeaways: The HGP sequenced all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA over 13 years
It revealed approximately 20,000 protein-coding genes in the human genome
The reference genome enables all subsequent human genomic research

faq.question: What surprised scientists most about the Human Genome Project results?
faq.answer: The number of protein-coding genes was shockingly low at roughly 20,000, far fewer than the 100,000 predicted. Humans have barely more genes than a roundworm. Much of the genome was once called junk DNA but is now known to contain important regulatory elements.

faq.question: How has the Human Genome Project impacted medicine?
faq.answer: It enabled pharmacogenomics for personalized drug prescribing, identification of disease-risk genes for predictive testing, development of targeted cancer therapies based on tumor genomics, and rapid pathogen sequencing for pandemic tracking and response.
